items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Search Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials (name-searchable), then view the certificate image for informant and parents' names, and find the burial/obituary entry in Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records (name-searchable) for parish and family plot companions.

Patrick's own marriage record (Pennsylvania, County Marriages and Pennsylvania, Marriages, both name-searchable) may state age, birthplace or parents; if church-recorded, it points to the Catholic parish in the Archdiocese of Philadelphia (loc_001: registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county). Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages and County Marriages, name-searchable; may instead have occurred in Ireland ca. 1840-45). Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) could die from 1850 to about 1890s or later, so the window follows his lifespan, not Patrick's. Pennsylvania, Probate Records is name-searchable but very thin, so also browse Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds images and the county's own probate index. Use Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings and Church Marriages (name-searchable); coal-region church films may be browse-only per loc_001, so browse images by parish if the index is empty.

Patrick was of age in the Civil War; Pennsylvania, Register of Military Volunteers and Grand Army of the Republic Membership Records are name-searchable and may give birthplace and age; a pension file (NARA) can name a widow, and a later mother or siblings.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick's death 12 Mar 1908 in Schuylkill County, sourced to a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), and that source is also cited on the Thomas-Patrick parent-child link. Re-read the certificate itself in Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (name-searchable) for the stated father and mother names, birthplace and informant. Death certificates are derivative on parentage (informant knowledge), so this gives a lead, not proof. Because loc_001 says statewide registration began 1906, 1908 is covered.

Patrick's own burial entry. The tree gives his birth as ~1845 in Ireland (from the 1850 census, age 5) while the question says Pennsylvania, so a baptism may not exist in a register we can reach and the birth parish is itself unknown. Burial and cemetery entries often give age, birthplace or parents. Search Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable), Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records (name-searchable). Catholic registers are held by the parish or Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001), so confirm the parish from the burial entry.

Timeline t_001 flags a medium gap 1851-1860 and the 1860 census is unsearched. The 1850 census (S1) already places Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, Schuylkill County (log_001); that is co-residence only, and 1850 does not state relationship. Search United States Census 1860 and 1870 (both name-searchable) for the household to show continuity, siblings, a mother's given name and birthplaces. Search Flynn variants (Flinn, Flin, Fflynn, O'Flynn).

The 1880 census is the first to record relationship to the head. If Patrick (about 35) or his widowed parent lived in a shared household, it states the relationship directly. United States Census 1880 is name-searchable. Also check where Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, tree) and Patrick lived, to place a parent near Patrick.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland per tree) to the candidate mother. It would confirm the couple as a unit, give her surname, and by its date relative to ~1845 corroborate Thomas as father, but it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Any surname found is not assumed to be her maiden name; she may have married earlier, so also look for her own record. Pre-1885 county marriage coverage is thin (loc_001: pre-1906 events rely on church records), so lead with SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, Pennsylvania, Church Marriages 1682-1976 and Pennsylvania, Marriages 1709-1940 (all name-searchable). Marriage may have occurred in Ireland, so widen to Irish records if no PA hit.

Patrick's baptism, if he was born in Pennsylvania as the question assumes. The tree says Ireland (1850 census), so this tests that conflict. Search SYNTH-PA-CHURCH and Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (both name-searchable) under the Flynn variants. Schuylkill County existed from 1811 so no parent-county split applies. A baptism naming parents would be direct evidence; a negative result supports an Irish birth and moves the search abroad.

Patrick's own marriage record, as the birth register may be out of reach. Marriage entries often give age, birthplace and sometimes parents' names. Search SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, Pennsylvania, Church Marriages 1682-1976 and, for 1885 onward, Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (all name-searchable). Witnesses are FAN leads.

Estate of Thomas Flynn (candidate father, b. ~1818 per tree). Window sized to the creator's lifespan: he could die anywhere from 1850 to about 1908 and later, not just within Patrick's life events. The county Register of Wills holds probate from 1811 and a will or administration naming heirs is a primary parentage source (loc_001). Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is name-searchable but thinly indexed, and Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds is name-searchable; try both, then the image browse item.

Because the probate index is thin, browse the Schuylkill County Register of Wills will and administration books and indexes directly (images via FamilySearch or the courthouse) for Thomas Flynn, and for Patrick as heir or administrator. Fallback for the name search if it returns nothing.

FAN item. Records of probable siblings and neighbors: baptisms, marriages and burials of other Flynn children with Thomas as father, plus sponsors and neighbors near dwelling 84 in the 1850 census. These can name the same parents and show the family unit, and a sibling's record may name a mother Patrick's own records omit. Use SYNTH-PA-CHURCH and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials (name-searchable); check the Mortality Schedules 1850-1880 (name-searchable) for a parent's death.

Obituary for Patrick Flynn after 12 Mar 1908 in Schuylkill County newspapers; it may name surviving siblings, birthplace in Ireland, and parents or a home parish. Not in the FamilySearch collections listed in loc_001 for 1908, so this runs in an external newspaper archive.

This plan is for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. He died in 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Records show a boy named Patrick, aged 5, living with a Thomas Flynn in 1850. But the family tree says he was born in Ireland, while the question says Pennsylvania, so the plan tests both. It starts with his 1908 death certificate and his burial record, which often name parents or a birthplace. Next come the 1860, 1870 and 1880 censuses, then the marriage of Thomas Flynn and the likely mother, Patrick's own baptism and marriage, and Thomas Flynn's will or estate papers. It also looks at siblings' and neighbors' records and a 1908 newspaper obituary. Church records are important here because Pennsylvania did not register births and deaths statewide until 1906.

Next, the FamilySearch collections will be searched in that order, starting with the death certificate. The courthouse probate books and the newspaper obituary will follow as separate steps.

items.rationale: Tree records Patrick's death 12 Mar 1908 in Schuylkill County, sourced to a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), and that source is also cited on the Thomas-Patrick parent-child link. Death certificates are derivative on parentage (informant knowledge), so this gives a lead, not proof. Because loc_001 says statewide registration began 1906, 1908 is covered.

Patrick's own burial entry. The tree gives his birth as ~1845 in Ireland (from the 1850 census, age 5) while the question says Pennsylvania, so a baptism may not exist in a register we can reach and the birth parish is itself unknown. Burial and cemetery entries often give age, birthplace or parents. Search Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable), Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records (name-searchable). Catholic registers are held by the parish or Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001), so confirm the parish from the burial entry.

Timeline t_001 flags a medium gap 1851-1860 and the 1860 census is unsearched. The 1850 census (S1) already places Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, Schuylkill County (log_001); that is co-residence only, and 1850 does not state relationship. Search United States Census 1860 and 1870 (both name-searchable) for the household to show continuity, siblings, a mother's given name and birthplaces. Search Flynn variants (Flinn, Flin, Fflynn, O'Flynn).

The 1880 census is the first to record relationship to the head. If Patrick (about 35) or his widowed parent lived in a shared household, it states the relationship directly. United States Census 1880 is name-searchable. Also check where Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, tree) and Patrick lived, to place a parent near Patrick.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland per tree) to the candidate mother. It would confirm the couple as a unit, give her surname, and by its date relative to ~1845 corroborate Thomas as father, but it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Any surname found is not assumed to be her maiden name; she may have married earlier, so also look for her own record. Pre-1885 county marriage coverage is thin (loc_001: pre-1906 events rely on church records), so lead with SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, Pennsylvania, Church Marriages 1682-1976 and Pennsylvania, Marriages 1709-1940 (all name-searchable). Marriage may have occurred in Ireland, so widen to Irish records if no PA hit.

Patrick's baptism, if he was born in Pennsylvania as the question assumes. The tree says Ireland (1850 census), so this tests that conflict. Search SYNTH-PA-CHURCH and Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (both name-searchable) under the Flynn variants. Schuylkill County existed from 1811 so no parent-county split applies. A baptism naming parents would be direct evidence; a negative result supports an Irish birth and moves the search abroad.

Patrick's own marriage record, as the birth register may be out of reach. Marriage entries often give age, birthplace and sometimes parents' names. Search SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, Pennsylvania, Church Marriages 1682-1976 and, for 1885 onward, Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (all name-searchable). Witnesses are FAN leads.

Estate of Thomas Flynn (candidate father, b. ~1818 per tree). Window sized to the creator's lifespan: he could die anywhere from 1850 to about 1908 and later, not just within Patrick's life events. The county Register of Wills holds probate from 1811 and a will or administration naming heirs is a primary parentage source (loc_001). Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is name-searchable but thinly indexed, and Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds is name-searchable; try both, then the image browse item.

Because the probate index is thin, browse the Schuylkill County Register of Wills will and administration books and indexes directly (images via FamilySearch or the courthouse) for Thomas Flynn, and for Patrick as heir or administrator. Fallback for the name search if it returns nothing.

FAN item. Records of probable siblings and neighbors: baptisms, marriages and burials of other Flynn children with Thomas as father, plus sponsors and neighbors near dwelling 84 in the 1850 census. These can name the same parents and show the family unit, and a sibling's record may name a mother Patrick's own records omit. Use SYNTH-PA-CHURCH and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials (name-searchable); check the Mortality Schedules 1850-1880 (name-searchable) for a parent's death.

Obituary for Patrick Flynn after 12 Mar 1908 in Schuylkill County newspapers; it may name surviving siblings, birthplace in Ireland, and parents or a home parish. Not in the FamilySearch collections listed in loc_001 for 1908, so this runs in an external newspaper archive.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

**Mode:** Add-new. The earlier plan for the question (pl_002) was already completed. I wrote a new active plan, pl_003. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**What the tree and records already hold:**
- **Patrick's birth:** The tree has a birth of about 1845 in Ireland, from the 1850 census.
- **Patrick's death:** The tree has a death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, from the death certificate.
- **Thomas Flynn:** The tree has Thomas Flynn as father, born about 1818 in Ireland, from the 1850 and 1860 census households and the death certificate.
- **1850 and 1860 censuses:** Patrick is age 5, then age 15, in Thomas's household. Relationship is only inferred from household position, because those censuses don't state it.
- **Death certificate:** The informant was a son-in-law, James Brown. It names Thomas as father but gives Patrick's birthplace as Pennsylvania. That conflicts with the censuses, which say Ireland.
- **Mother:** Nothing in the project names her.
- **FamilySearch hints and Patrick's profile:** I did not review pending FamilySearch hints or read his FamilySearch profile. He is the project's subject, and the tree entry has no FamilySearch link.

**pl_003 items, in order (all in Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States):**
- **pli_006:** Census, FamilySearch, 1870–1880. Find Thomas's household and Patrick's own household and neighbors. The 1880 census is the first to state relationship to the head, and these records should show the wife's name.
- **pli_007:** Marriage records, FamilySearch, 1865–1900. Patrick's marriage and his daughters' marriages, including James Brown's. These name spouses and witnesses.
- **pli_008:** Church records, other repository, 1845–1908. Catholic registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county. Children's baptisms and marriages name sponsors and witnesses.
- **pli_009:** Marriage records, FamilySearch, 1830–1850. This is the dedicated item for Thomas's marriage to the mother. The mother's surname may be a prior married name, so it isn't assumed to be her maiden name. The marriage also would not by itself prove Patrick is their child.
- **pli_010:** Probate, county courthouse, 1860–1910. Thomas's estate, and Patrick's own. It would name heirs, executors and creditors. The FamilySearch probate collection is browse-only (personCount 0).
- **pli_011:** Cemetery and burial records, FamilySearch, 1860–1908. This is Patrick's own burial entry, since a baptism may not exist in reach for an Irish birth around 1845. It also shows adjacent Flynn burials.
- **pli_012:** Newspaper, other repository, 1908. Patrick's obituary should list surviving siblings and in-laws.
- **pli_013:** Naturalization, FamilySearch, 1850–1906. Thomas's papers would name witnesses and his Irish origin.

None of the items is a fallback for another.

Patrick Flynn's parents are still unproven. Censuses and his death certificate point to a father named Thomas Flynn, but nothing names his mother, and the records disagree on whether Patrick was born in Ireland or Pennsylvania. The new plan looks at the people around him instead of only at him: neighbors, his wife and daughters, his son-in-law James Brown, and church sponsors. It starts with later censuses and marriage records. Then it moves to church records, the marriage of Thomas and his wife, estate papers, burial records, his 1908 obituary, and naturalization papers. Any of these could name his mother or siblings, or show where the family came from.

Next, I'd search the 1870 and 1880 censuses for Thomas's household and Patrick's own household and neighbors, then the marriage records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Also search brother Patrick Sheahan (tree: purchased land in Schuylkill County 1875, Deed Book 42 p. 118) and a household of Sheahans, since Michael may have lodged with kin. Try variants Sheehan, Shehan, Shean, Sheean.

FAN item. Tree records Patrick Sheahan, brother of Michael (shared parent I3), buying land from James Kelly in Schuylkill County in 1875 (S1, Deed Book 42 p. 118), seven years before Michael's move: a brother already settled there suggests kin-assisted migration rather than only job-seeking. Search Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds (name-searchable) and Recorder of Deeds images for Michael, Patrick and James Kelly (grantor, possible neighbour or employer contact) 1875-1895 for deeds, leases or witnesses linking them. loc_001 notes coal-region laborers often leased rather than purchased, so absence of a Michael deed is expected and not negative evidence.

Michael's and Patrick's marriages and their children's baptisms in Schuylkill parishes would date arrival and may name sponsors who are kin or earlier settlers. Search Pennsylvania Church Marriages, Civil/County Marriages and Births and Christenings (all name-searchable). Per loc_001, Catholic registers sit with the parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia (Schuylkill stayed under it), not the county, and statewide civil registration began only in 1906, so parish registers are the main source; some are browse-only image groups to browse image by image.

The 1882 directory (log_002) is the only record of Michael as a miner. Search U.S. City and Business Directories (name-searchable) for Michael across 1880-1890 to bracket the year he first appears in Schuylkill County, the town and colliery area, and whether his occupation changes (laborer, miner, mine laborer). Confirms continuity across the 1870-1882 gap instead of assuming it from name alone.

Direct context for the cause: local papers (e.g. Pottsville papers; to be located via a newspaper-archive search on the researcher's own subscription sites) report colliery openings, hiring, strikes and migration of labour from farming districts around 1880-1884, and may name Michael in a mine accident, employment or arrival notice. Treated as context, not proof of his individual motive. Also check Michael's death notice or obituary (after 1882) which may state when and why he came.

Occupational records: Pennsylvania mine inspectors' annual reports (Schuylkill districts), colliery and coal-company employment/payroll records (e.g. Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, held in archives such as Hagley), and mine accident reports may name Michael as employee or casualty and the colliery that hired him, the most direct test of the coal-mining motive. Repository and holdings to be confirmed by the researcher on the archive's own site; none cited from memory.

Tree gives no birthplace for Michael or Patrick; the surname suggests Irish origin, unverified. If he was foreign-born, naturalization petitions (county courts; some coal-region films are browse-only per loc_001) state arrival date and residence and show whether he came straight to the coal region. Search naturalization collections for Michael and Patrick, with image browse of Schuylkill County court records as the fallback if name search fails.

Michael's own death/burial record (Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, Cemetery Records, probate and obituary sources; no statewide death certificates before 1906) may give age, birthplace, years of residence and mining occupation, and probate or estate papers may name relatives and former residence. Window runs to a plausible death date well after 1882. Probate collection is only minimally name-searchable, so browse county Register of Wills images as the fallback.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Survival is uncertain, so this is a finding-aid inquiry first.

The tree holds no death for Michael. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Search Sheahan with variants Sheehan, Shehan, Sheahen, Shean.

Tree fact F1 records only a 1870 residence in Pennsylvania, and log_001 says the household was a farmer's outside Schuylkill County. Re-read that 1870 entry in full: the county, neighbors, household members and any relatives or in-laws whose later presence in the coal region would show chain migration. 1870 names every household member but not relationships. Name-searchable, 1870 collection.

log_002 came from a city/county directory (US City and Business Directories, name-searchable). Directories before and after 1882 show the year he first appears as a miner, his town (colliery district), and changes of employer or occupation. This bounds the move date and tests whether he stayed in mining, since the 1890 census is not available.

Marriages, baptisms of children and burials place the family by date and parish. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, County Marriages and Church Marriages are name-searchable; coal-region Catholic registers sit with the Philadelphia archdiocese (parish-held, per loc_001) and some church films are browse-only. A child born outside the county before 1882 and another inside it afterward brackets the move and may state the father's occupation. Note that statewide civil registration began only in 1906, so church records stand in for births before then. Also check his marriage: a marriage in a non-coal county vs. Schuylkill speaks to timing.

Local coal-region newspapers (e.g. Pottsville papers) reported colliery openings, hiring drives, strikes and mine accidents by name, and could name Michael or his employer and neighborhood. Identify digitized runs (Chronicling America, Newspapers.com or a Pottsville library) from the repositories' own sites; not yet confirmed which are available.

Employment-side records: coal company payrolls and employee ledgers (the large coal-and-railroad companies of the region), and the annual Pennsylvania mine inspectors' reports listing miners injured or killed. These would directly document mining employment, the strongest test of the family tradition. Locate the holding archives and finding aids; availability and repository must be confirmed on the archives' own sites.

The question notes no land purchase has been found. Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds is name-searchable but sparse for Schuylkill; loc_001 says coal-region laborers often leased company land rather than buying. Search for a sale of his former farm in the 1870 county (financing a move) and any Schuylkill purchase or lease. Sale of a farm with a later miner residence would support a work-driven move.

Michael's own death or burial entry, and obituaries and cemetery records, may state occupation (miner, black lung, accident), birthplace and years in the county. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and Cemetery Records are name-searchable. Pre-1906 deaths have no civil record, so rely on church burials, cemeteries and probate.

FAN item: siblings, in-laws or neighbors named Sheahan or from his 1870 neighborhood who also appear in 1880 Schuylkill censuses, marriages or church records. Kin already working in the mines would show a family pull to the coal region; this tests the tradition about why he moved.

output.text_response:
**Mode:** Add-new. The earlier plan for q_001 (pl_002) was already completed, and its items were the 1860 census and the 1908 death record. The new plan is **pl_003**, written for q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

---

**Already recorded in the tree and logs:**
- The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland, from the 1850 census. The question text says Pennsylvania, so the plan tests both.
- The 1850 census shows Patrick aged 5 in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill household, dwelling 84.
- The 1860 census shows Patrick aged 15 in Thomas's household, dwelling 112.
- The 1908-03-12 death certificate, Schuylkill County, names Thomas Flynn as father. The informant was son-in-law James Brown.
- Thomas Flynn (I2) is recorded with a birth of about 1818 in Ireland, and nothing else.
- The timeline marks 1860 to 1908 as a high gap, with the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses all missing.
- Patrick has no FamilySearch ark on file, so there are no hints to review.

---

**pl_003 items, in order:**

1. **pli_006** — Census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, **1870**. Name search for Patrick and Thomas with spelling variants. (1870 does not record relationship to head, so a shared household only suggests kinship.)
2. **pli_007** — Census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, **1880**. First census to record relationship to head — Patrick listed as Thomas's son would be direct evidence.
3. **pli_008** — Census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, **1900**. Gives birth month/year, immigration year, and naturalization status. (1890 census is effectively lost, making 1900 the only bridge between 1880 and his death.)
4. **pli_009** — Mortality schedules, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, **1870–1880**. If Thomas drops out of the census record, this shows when he died.
5. **pli_010** — Vital record (Patrick's marriage), Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, **1860–1908**. Marriage records may name his parents.
6. **pli_011** — Church or marriage record for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother, FamilySearch, **1818–1900**. Would give the mother's name. Catholic registers sit at parish or diocese level; some are browse-only.
7. **pli_012** — Probate (Thomas Flynn's will or administration), Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, **1860–1900**. Would name his heirs. Collection is name-searchable but small; image browse may be needed.

---

**Summary:** This plan bridges the 1860–1908 gap by searching the three available post-1860 censuses for Patrick as an adult (and Thomas with him), then checks when Thomas died, and rounds out with Patrick's marriage record, Thomas's marriage record, and Thomas's probate papers — together aiming to establish household relationships, the mother's name, and any named heirs.

**Next step:** Search the 1870 census for Patrick and Thomas Flynn (pli_006), then proceed to 1880 and 1900.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Search Patrick (~35) and Thomas (~62) with name variants, also in neighboring coal-region counties in case of moves. Wife and children seen here also feed the 1900 search.

'United States, Census, 1900' is name-searchable; it gives Patrick's birth month/year, immigration year, years married and naturalization status, and relationship to head. Patrick (~55) is alive until 1908; Thomas (~82) may live with him as an aged father. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only the subject's birth (20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup) with no source and no parents. The baptism entry names both parents. loc_001: the parish register is only ~3% name-indexed, and the 1763-1814 register volume covers 1779, so the baptism should exist; try a name search in Denmark, Church Books (name-searchable), then browse the register images for Aug-Sep 1779. Search variants Mikkel/Michel/Mikkels, Nielsen/Nielsøn/Nielsen Blyeberg (Blyeberg may be a farm/byname, not a surname, per Denmark Naming Customs). Patronymic only gives father's given name Niels, not which Niels.

Per the Denmark Military Records page and loc_001, levying rolls from 1788/89 list every male from birth under his father's name, so a roll entry for Mikkel (aged ~10 in 1789) is direct parentage evidence independent of the baptism. Denmark, Military Levying Rolls 1789-1861 is name-searchable; search Mikkel Nielsen and Niels with a son born 1779, noting the roll's parish number and father's name. Place fields may rank rather than filter, so check Stagstrup/Thisted Amt hits manually.

Fallback if the indexed roll search underdelivers: browse the Thisted Amt levying roll volume (image group 004748896, browse-only, personCount 0 / 0% indexed) for the Stagstrup parish section, finding Mikkel (b. 1779) beneath his father.

Denmark Census 1787-1930 is name-searchable. The 1787 and 1801 censuses list whole households with relationships, so a boy Mikkel aged 8 (1787) or 22 (1801) in a household headed by a Niels places him with a candidate father and gives the father's age and occupation. Places the child with the household, unlike a marriage record alone.

Dedicated item for the marriage of the candidate parents (Niels and the mother named in the baptism) to each other. It confirms them as a couple, supplies the mother's name (possibly a patronymic, and she may have had an earlier marriage, so do not treat any surname as settled), and its date relative to 1779 corroborates the baptism. It does not by itself prove Mikkel is their child. The register volume starts 1763, so a marriage before that may sit in an earlier volume or another parish; check neighbouring parishes if absent.

FAN item: siblings' baptisms (same parents, 1763-1814) and the godparents/sponsors named in Mikkel's and his siblings' baptisms. Sponsors are frequently kin and help separate the several men named Niels in the parish and confirm the father's household.

Objective also asks when the father died. Burial entries in the Stagstrup church book for the candidate Niels (age at death, farm, wife) from 1779 to about 1840 (father could live ~60 years past the birth). Window sized to the father's lifespan, not the subject's.

Father's estate (skifte) would name heirs including Mikkel and date the father's death. Denmark, Probate Indexes 1674-1851 is name-searchable; the Hassing Herred skifteprotokoller volume (image group 004392710) is browse-only (personCount 0). Window runs to 1851 because the father's death may be up to ~60 years after 1779; verify that Stagstrup lay in Hassing Herred before browsing.

Subject's own marriage and death/burial entries, which may give age, birthplace and sometimes his father's name; useful to confirm identity (Blyeberg byname) and trace him if he left Stagstrup. The baptism is expected to exist (register 1763-1814 covers 1779), so this is corroboration rather than a substitute.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

Browse Muhlenberg probate volumes for administrator bonds, estate settlements and register entries bracketing the death. Window set by his own lifespan from 1870 (he would be 56) allowing for settlement filed years after death.

County death registers (Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970, collection 1804888) cover 1852-1910 but loc_001 says 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. Search for Elijah Wilkins with variants (Wilkens, Wilkin, Elijah/Elisha) for a register entry giving date, place, age and parents.

The question presupposes death certificates, so test it: Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (collection 1417491). A death after 1 January 1911 would make him about 97, unlikely but must be excluded; also, certificates of his children (1911 onward) name father Elijah Wilkins and his birthplace, helping confirm identity and identify heirs.

The 1870 residence is the last-known-alive date. The 1880 census (records relationship to head and birthplace) shows whether Elijah is present, or a widow or household headed by another; absence brackets death to 1870-1880. Also check the 1880 mortality schedule for deaths in the year before June 1880.

loc_001 notes church burial registers and cemetery records can bracket the death. Search Muhlenberg cemetery transcriptions, Find a Grave and church burial registers for Elijah Wilkins (b. c. 1814); gravestone dates give an exact death date and place.

FAN item: land deeds and tax lists in which Wilkins heirs or neighbors convey his land 'heirs of Elijah Wilkins, deceased' fix a death before the deed date and name heirs; tax lists show the last year he was assessed. Window runs from the 1870 residence through heirs' later conveyances.
Local newspaper obituaries or death notices may state the date and place of death and family; used to corroborate findings from probate and registers.

## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Mary Dawson (I1), female, birth about 1772, Lincolnshire, no parents, no sources, no FamilySearch ark. A baptism naming parents is the direct answer. loc_001 flags England Births and Christenings (1473014) as a partial Legacy index: a nil is not proof of absence. Search Dawson with variants (Dawsen, Dowson, Dason) and Mary with Maria/Polly, then verify against the parish register image. Baptism may be a few years either side of 1772.

Fallback for the index search: browse parish register images and Bishop's Transcripts for candidate Lincolnshire parishes once the parish is narrowed by her marriage or census residence. Records stay with the creating parish and the Lincoln diocese, so check both the register and the transcript for gaps.

Mary's own marriage (age about 18-33) is unknown in the tree. Parish marriage entries or licences/bonds may give age, parish of origin, father's name if a minor, and witnesses who may be kin. Supplies her residence and married name to anchor later searches, and compensates for a baptism that may not be indexed or may predate register survival.

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (a Dawson couple in the parish identified above, about 1750-1771). It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's maiden name if it was her first marriage (not assumed), and show timing relative to Mary's birth. It does not itself prove Mary is their child; that needs the baptism or a record naming her with them. Search for earlier marriages of the mother too if a remarriage appears.

FAN item: baptisms of other Dawson children to the same couple in the same parish (siblings), and sponsors or witnesses. Sibling entries naming parents establish the household that Mary's baptism would belong to, and help when her own entry is lost or mis-indexed.

Mary's own burial entry. A baptism may not exist or be indexed: the locality guide gives no parish register start date, so the birth parish is unconfirmed. Burial entries often give age and abode; later ones sometimes give more. Window runs from her likely adult life through age about 83, set by her lifespan.

If Mary survived to age about 69-79, the 1851 census records birthplace (parish and county) and the 1841 census gives age and county-born flag. Birthplace gives the parish to search for the baptism. Ages in 1841 are rounded, so treat as approximate. Check the 1851 first because it gives birthplace.

Wills of a candidate father Dawson (death possible from 1772 to about 1832, set by the father's lifespan, born about 1725-1750) or of Mary's husband naming her. A will naming daughter Mary with a married name would link her to the parents. Check the Lincoln consistory and archdeaconry courts and the Prerogative Court of Canterbury.

Paid repositories (Ancestry, FindMyPast, MyHeritage) hold Lincolnshire parish register transcripts and images that may differ from FamilySearch's partial Legacy index. Search after the free items so as to follow up with target parishes and surname variants.

## Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico - 1880-1920

Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org)

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Birth about 1895, Guadalajara (no parents, no sources). Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 is name-searchable; a civil birth act names both parents. Search paternal surname Hernández alone first (loc_001 quirk: indexed records often carry only the first surname), then search by parent surnames Hernández and Ramírez without the child's name. Treat Hernández Ramírez as father's then mother's surname per Mexico Naming Customs, but allow reversed or conflated forms. Verify against the image.

The baptism names parents and godparents. Mexico, Jalisco, Catholic Church Records, 1590-2022 and Mexico, Baptisms, 1560-1950 are both name-searchable. Search Hernández first-surname only, with María Guadalupe and variants (Guadalupe, Lupe, Ma. Guadalupe; first name María often dropped per naming customs), then parent-based searches. Guadalajara had several parishes, so do not restrict to one; birth is only 'about' 1895, so widen the window if needed.

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (civil in Jalisco Civil Registration and church in Jalisco Catholic Church Records; Mexico, Marriages, 1570-1950 is name-searchable but small by person count, so add an image browse as its fallback). It confirms the couple as a unit, gives the mother's maiden surname (Mexican women keep maiden names, but verify, and check for remarriage), and its date against about 1895 corroborates parentage. It does not by itself prove María Guadalupe is their child; that needs the birth or baptism in items 1-2. Run after a candidate couple is found, or search by surnames Hernández and Ramírez.

Subject's own marriage (civil and church) is the next route if the birth or baptism is missing or unindexed; marriage acts state age, birthplace and parents' names. Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration and Catholic Church Records cover it name-searchable. Spouse unknown, so search the subject by name with Guadalajara and Jalisco-wide, using variants of Guadalupe.

Subject's own death or burial entry, dated after she was last known alive. Birth about 1895 may not match a located baptism, so death acts (civil registration runs to 2000; Mexico, Deaths, 1680-1940 is name-searchable) often name parents and an age. Death place unknown, so search Jalisco-wide and widen if absent.

FAN item: siblings' baptisms and births (and their godparents) found by searching parents' surnames Hernández and Ramírez with no child name. A sibling's record naming the same couple, in the same parish and decade, bears directly on who María Guadalupe's parents were and may expose the correct parish. Window set by the parents' childbearing years around 1895.

Window follows the creators' lifespans: parents of a child born 1895 can die from then to roughly 1955 or later, not just within the subject's own window. Use only after candidates are identified from items 1-3 and 6.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Baptisms of Patrick and his siblings. The 1845 birth may predate any local register or occur in Ireland (tree and objective disagree), so the baptism may not exist. **Mode:** supersede. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**What was false:** pl_002 assumed Thomas Flynn died in 1870-1890. Its unfinished probate item (pli_006) was dated 1870-1890. The new reference puts his death near 1865. I superseded pl_002 and kept it as the audit trail. Its two completed items (1860 census and the 1908 death certificate) stay as they were.

**Already in the tree:**
- Patrick (I1): born about 1845 in Ireland, which conflicts with the objective's "Pennsylvania". Died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County.
- The 1860 census (log_004) shows Patrick, age 15, in Thomas's household.
- The death certificate (log_005) names Thomas as father. The informant was his son-in-law, James Brown. No mother is named.
- Thomas (I2): born about 1818 in Ireland, with no death fact recorded.
- Mary (I3) and James (I4): children of Thomas, from the St. Mary's, Pottsville baptismal registers.
- None of these people has a FamilySearch link, so I added no hints-review item.

**New plan pl_003, in order:**
1. pli_007, probate, Schuylkill County, 1860-1870, FamilySearch. This is the carried-forward probate item with the corrected window. It uses the name-searchable Wills and Deeds, plus an image browse of the county docket as fallback, since the Probate Records collection holds very few names.
2. pli_008, church burial and cemetery, 1860-1870, FamilySearch. This is Thomas's own burial entry. Mortality schedules likely miss a 1865 death.
3. pli_009, 1870 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It should show a widow or an adult son as head of household, which would name the mother.
4. pli_010, parents' marriage, 1835-1845, FamilySearch. It is a dedicated item for Thomas and Patrick's mother. It gives her maiden name only if this was her first marriage. It does not prove Patrick is their child, and it fails if they married in Ireland.
5. pli_011, baptisms, Pottsville, 1840-1860, FamilySearch. Patrick's baptism may not exist, because the birth may predate the register or have been in Ireland. The entries for Mary and James are already cited, so the item checks what they say about the mother. Patrick's own death record is already found.
6. pli_012, siblings' and Patrick's marriage and death records, 1860-1900, FamilySearch. This is the item covering relatives and associates. These records may name the parents, including the mother.

None of the items is a fallback for another. All six are for FamilySearch, so the next step is to hand them to search-records.

---

I replaced the old search plan for Patrick Flynn's parents. It looked for Thomas Flynn's will in 1870-1890, but the new reference says he died around 1865. The new plan starts with Thomas's will or estate papers from 1860-1870, and then his burial record. After that it looks at the 1870 census for a widow or grown son heading the household, because that would name Patrick's mother. It then covers the parents' marriage, the church baptisms in Pottsville, and the marriage and death records of Patrick's siblings, which may name both parents. One thing to know: the family tree says Patrick was born in Ireland, but the research goal says Pennsylvania. So a baptism record may not exist, and the burial and marriage records matter more.

Next, I'll search FamilySearch for these records in that order.
